CLAUDE.md

Source: CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

What this is

zuregex is PCRE2 packaged twice. For R code it is a set of re_* verbs that do what base R’s perl = TRUE engine cannot: a compiled-pattern cache, OpenMP matching, captures filled in C, PCRE2’s full replacement language and per-call match limits. For C code it is a library that sibling packages reach through LinkingTo instead of vendoring their own PCRE2. The engine is a vendored PCRE2, 8-bit with JIT, one version on every platform, with hidden symbols because R already loads its own libpcre2-8. No Imports: zero hard runtime dependencies. It makes no linear-time promise (CRAN’s re2 does), adds no pattern syntax, and does not ship the 16-bit or 32-bit libraries, pcre2grep or pcre2test.

The specification is .agents/design.md, adopted from RFC 0042 in pedrobtz/packages. It outranks this file: CLAUDE.md orients, the design decides. Its decisions (§13) are settled; its open questions (§15) stay open until the roadmap or a stage settles them.

Current state

PCRE2 10.48 is vendored and builds on every platform (Stage 1). Patterns compile, with flags, dialects and a cache (Stage 2). re_detect() and re_count() match, serially, through the three-phase core (Stage 3), and re_locate() and re_locate_all() locate (Stage 4), and the extract and match verbs capture (Stage 5). re_replace(), re_expand() and re_split() complete the v0.1.0 verbs (Stage 6), and re_limits() bounds every one of them (Stage 7). Phase 2 runs on OpenMP threads (Stage 8). The roadmap in .agents/roadmap.md takes it to v0.1.0; §11 of the design lists the stages it is expected to hold.

Stage tracking

Progress toward the next version is tracked as GitHub sub-issues, so the parent issue shows a progress bar such as “6 of 7”.

  • One parent issue per target version, titled with the bare version, for example v0.1.0. v0.1.0 issue: created by pkg-roadmap.
  • One sub-issue per roadmap stage, titled as the roadmap titles it, for example Stage 3 — R interface, and linking to that section. The number of stages is whatever the roadmap has; there is no fixed scale.
  • Every tracking issue carries the stage label, so it can be told apart from bug and feature issues and left out of open-issue counts.
  • Close a stage by merging its pull request. Put Closes #<n> in the body of the stage’s pull request. Never close a stage whose exit criteria are not met; record a deviation in the roadmap first.
  • The roadmap stays authoritative. The issues record which stages are done, not what a stage requires. Adding, removing or renaming a stage means editing the roadmap and the sub-issues in the same change.
  • Each stage has a CI tier, quick or full. The roadmap sets it, and quick is the default. See Continuous integration for what each means. The second-to-last stage, Full CI, runs the full set and fixes what it finds before v0.1.0 readiness.
  • Close the parent issue when CRAN accepts the version and it is tagged. Opening a parent issue implies at least one stage sub-issue; a parent with no sub-issues shows no progress on the board.

Versioning

A new package develops at 0.0.0.9000 and targets 0.1.0 for its first CRAN release. Set Version: 0.1.0 and the matching NEWS.md heading when the package enters Pre-flight. Bump to 0.1.0.9000 only after CRAN accepts it, never before: a .9000 version above an unreleased 0.1.0 heading is wrong.

Until the first release the R API may change freely. Sibling packages can still depend on this one before CRAN does, through Remotes: or LinkingTo:. The design (§3) names four consumers of the C API: vectorscan, which drops its own PCRE2 copy for it, and the planned zutoken, zuschema and zupeg. A change to the C API, a header in inst/include/ or a static archive breaks them even before 0.1.0. A package that others wait on should reach CRAN first.

Commands

Run from the package root.

Rscript -e 'devtools::load_all()'                # compile src/ and load
Rscript -e 'devtools::document()'                # roxygen -> NAMESPACE, man/
Rscript -e 'devtools::test()'                    # full testthat suite
Rscript -e 'devtools::test(filter = "<name>")'   # one test file
Rscript -e 'devtools::test(shuffle = TRUE)'      # order independence
Rscript -e 'devtools::check()'                   # R CMD check
air format .                                     # format R sources
tools/vendor/verify              # vendored tree = upstream + declared patches
tools/vendor/verify --offline    # the same without re-deriving from upstream
tools/vendor/fetch               # re-vendor from tools/vendor/manifest.tsv

The benchmark harness arrives with its stage; add it here when it does.

Architecture

Written as stages land; see .agents/design.md §4 for the planned shape, a three-phase split where only the middle, OpenMP phase runs without the R API.

  • src/init.c registers the .Call routines and is the only exported symbol, R_init_zuregex, marked attribute_visible.
  • src/zuregex.h declares the first-party native routines.
  • src/info.c backs zuregex_info().
  • src/vendor/pcre2/ is PCRE2 with its upstream layout; src/Makevars.in lists its 31 units in PCRE2_OBJECTS and builds it without CMake. ./configure writes src/Makevars from it, choosing the OpenMP flags as zurand does, and ./configure.win writes src/Makevars.win. Edit Makevars.in, never the generated files. src/pcre2-config/config.h is the package’s own PCRE2 configuration.
  • src/pattern.c turns flag letters into PCRE2 options and owns zuregex_pattern, a compiled pattern with a reference count. src/pattern.h has no R API, so later stages can read patterns from worker threads.
  • src/cache.c is the LRU pattern cache; src/compile.c holds the R entry points for re_compile(), re_info() and the cache.
  • An re object is a list of external pointers, each holding one reference, with the pattern, flags, dialect, literal and jit as attributes. re_restore() recompiles pointers that saveRDS() nulled.
  • R/errors.R has zuregex_abort() and the argument checks.
  • src/match.h defines the three phases every verb shares. zuregex_collect() is phase 1: subjects become pointer and length pairs, translated to UTF-8 where needed, and patterns become a table plus a per-element index. Phase 2 loops in src/match.c read only those arrays. Phase 3 turns per-element status into R results or a condition.
  • R/match.R applies the pairing rule (patterns()), decides between UTF-8 and bytes (subjects()), and raises match errors. R/detect.R and R/locate.R hold the verbs.
  • zuregex_next_start() in src/match.c is the one place that decides where the next search starts: PCRE2’s empty-match rule, JavaScript’s, or one character on for overlap. Every iterating verb uses it.
  • src/capture.c keeps every group’s offsets per match in phase 2. make_string() there is the one place a match becomes a CHARSXP, marked UTF-8 for character input and bytes for bytes. group_layout() in R/capture.R builds the column union for per-element patterns.
  • src/replace.c builds each replacement from the match just found, with pcre2_substitute() and PCRE2_SUBSTITUTE_MATCHED, so n, both empty-match rules and re_expand() share one loop. A replacement function’s strings are spliced in by the same loop, in match order. re_split() is a builder over the capture scan in src/capture.c.
  • tools/oracles/python-re.py records Python’s results for tests/testthat/test-python.R.
  • Limits reach C as one double vector (match, depth, heap, on_limit), made by call_limits() in R/limits.R. zuregex_collect() turns it into a PCRE2 match context whose memory comes from R_alloc(), so it needs no freeing. A replacement function makes two passes; R passes each element’s first row to the second, so a limited element cannot misalign the strings.
  • src/omp.h gates OpenMP on ZUREGEX_OPENMP and defines ZUREGEX_OMP_PARALLEL and ZUREGEX_OMP_FOR, the shape of every phase-2 loop: per-thread match data inside the parallel block, dynamic scheduling, and the thread count in a variable named nt. src/threads.c holds the cap and the serial threshold.
  • src/locate.c converts byte offsets to one-based characters in phase 2. Per-element match lists are malloc()ed, and phase 3 runs under R_ExecWithCleanup() so they are freed even if an R allocation fails.

Invariants that are easy to break

These are the constraints the design already fixes. Add each new one when a stage establishes it.

  • Zero hard runtime dependencies. DESCRIPTION has no Imports. Anything beyond base R goes in Suggests and is guarded.
  • The OpenMP phase never touches the R API (design §4). STRING_ELT, translation and allocation can allocate or run R code, so they belong in the serial phases before and after. A call into R from a worker thread is a crash that only shows up under load.
  • Results are identical for any thread count (design §6.6). Tests cap at two threads in tests/testthat/setup.R; a result that depends on the cap is a bug, not a tuning question. test-threads.R runs every verb at one thread and at the cap.
  • Phase-2 loops share no mutable state. Running out of memory is recorded in the element’s own status as PCRE2_ERROR_NOMEMORY, never in a shared flag, and loops never break out of the element loop.
  • The pattern cache is main-thread only (design §6.4). It has no lock because nothing else reads or writes it. Touching it from phase 2 breaks that assumption silently.
  • Vendored PCRE2 symbols are hidden (design §4). R has its own libpcre2-8 loaded, so an exported symbol can bind to R’s copy, a different version with different behaviour.
  • Two offset conventions, deliberately (design §6.2). R results are one-based, inclusive and in characters; the C API is zero-based, half-open and in bytes. Convert at the boundary, never in the middle.
  • A pattern’s reference count is main-thread only. The cache, each re external pointer and its finalizer own references. A worker thread may read a zuregex_pattern, never retain or release one.
  • Bytes mode needs patterns compiled without PCRE2_UTF. The key’s utf field separates the two in the cache. An re object is always compiled for UTF-8 and is recompiled for bytes when a call needs it.
  • PCRE2 is built with LINK_SIZE 4 (src/pcre2-config/config.h). With upstream’s 2, patterns well under the cache’s 65,536-character limit fail to compile.
  • The C API uses opaque handles (design §7), so a PCRE2 upgrade never breaks a consumer’s build. Exposing a raw pcre2_code in inst/include/zuregex.h ties every consumer to one PCRE2 version.

Testing conventions

  • Self-sufficient. Every test builds its own inputs inside the test_that() block. No file-scope objects.
  • Self-contained. Global state goes through withr::local_*(), randomised input through withr::local_seed(). Tests write only under tempdir().
  • Assert on condition classes, never message text. Use expect_error(..., class = "<pkg>_<kind>_error"). Wording belongs in snapshot tests.
  • Order independence. devtools::test(shuffle = TRUE) is part of the definition of done.
  • Borrow a conformance suite before writing one. Mainstream implementations in Python, Java, Go or Node usually ship a test corpus. Use it as an oracle rather than inventing cases by hand. The design (§9) names two oracles: PCRE2’s own testdata/ through the C API, and base R’s perl = TRUE and stringr for parity, with every deliberate difference marked # GAP. Base R and stringr parity is wired up through helper-corpus.R; the testdata/ oracle arrives with Stage 9.
  • Helpers live in tests/testthat/helper-*.R. helper-symbols.R runs nm on the loaded shared object; helper-types.R has small predicates; helper-cache.R gives a test its own cache (local_cache()); helper-corpus.R is the parity corpus every verb is checked on.
  • Timing tests are opt-in. skip_unless_timing() runs them only with ZUREGEX_TIMING_TESTS=true, which R-CMD-check.yaml sets. Coverage, sanitizers, valgrind and gctorture distort timings. The thread speedup test also needs ZUREGEX_BENCH_THREADS=true and four free cores, which GitHub’s shared runners do not have.
  • Keep the suite inside the CRAN time budget. About 4 seconds on a 2026 laptop at Stage 4, timing tests off. Re-measure when a stage adds a large corpus.

Definition of done

devtools::document() and devtools::check() clean, meaning 0 errors, 0 warnings and 0 notes. The one allowed note is “New submission” before the first release. devtools::test(shuffle = TRUE) green. CI green at the change’s tier: the quick profile for a quick roadmap stage or an ordinary pull request, the full profile for a full stage, Full CI, and every release. A user-facing change also needs a test, roxygen documentation and a NEWS.md entry.

Releasing to CRAN

  • CI is the pre-submission check. The pedrobtz/r-actions R CMD check runs --as-cran on the CRAN-like runners and containers, and it replaces win-builder, the macOS builder and R-hub. None of them is a release step, and cran-comments.md lists the CI legs as its test environments.
  • Entering Pre-flight. The roadmap’s feature stages are done, the version is set as in Versioning, NEWS.md and cran-comments.md are written, and CI is green. Only submission work remains.
  • Before submitting, run pkg-critical-review once the roadmap is implemented and fix what it files, then pkg-cran-review, and resolve every finding. Both skills are in pedrobtz/r-skills.
  • The pretest is automated and does not read cran-comments.md. A NOTE that is explained but not fixed gets the upload archived. Fix the NOTE, as under Vendored native code, instead of justifying it.
  • After acceptance, pkg-post-cran tags the submitted commit with the bare version, 0.1.0 (no v), publishes the GitHub release, bumps to 0.1.0.9000, closes the version’s parent issue and moves the board card.

Editing rules

  • roxygen comments are the source. Never edit man/ or NAMESPACE by hand.
  • Edit README.Rmd, not the generated README.md.
  • Keep prose simple and short. One idea per sentence.
  • Wrap roxygen text at 80 characters and run air format . on R sources.
  • Use lower_snake_case, and prefix internal native symbols with <pkg>_.
  • Keep hard runtime dependencies at zero unless a recorded design decision says otherwise.
  • Export and document public functions. Do not create roxygen topics for internal ones.

Continuous integration

Workflows come from pedrobtz/r-actions. Call those reusable workflows instead of writing bespoke ones, and pin a released tag rather than main. Pin a workflow that holds a write token, such as coverage.yml, to a commit, with the tag in a comment. The R-CMD-check workflow must call r-cmd-check.yml, because a hand-rolled one does not count as the pre-submission check. This package calls r-cmd-check.yml from .github/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml, with the quick/full profile chosen by event and the full-ci label, and coverage.yml from .github/workflows/coverage.yaml. The pkgdown site is built by .github/workflows/pkgdown.yaml, the r-lib/actions example workflow.

A ruleset requires pull requests on main, so the coverage badge cannot be committed there. coverage.yaml sets badge-branch: gh-pages, and the pkgdown deploy sets force: false so it rebases over the badge commit instead of overwriting it. Keep both, and keep the README badge pointing at gh-pages/badges/coverage.svg.

Small edits get a small run. The shared workflows look at the files a pull request changes, compared with its merge base:

  • Markdown only, such as README.md, NEWS.md or cran-comments.md, skips every check. Only coverage and the pkgdown site run.
  • DESCRIPTION or README.Rmd as well, and nothing else, adds one R CMD check on Ubuntu R-release.
  • Any other file runs everything.

So put a README or DESCRIPTION touch-up in its own pull request. Once a pull request changes code, every later push to it runs every workflow.

Quick by default, full by exception

The full profile is slow. gctorture at step 20 alone has taken 36 to 107 minutes on sibling packages. Waiting on it between roadmap stages was the main thing slowing roadmaps down, so:

  • Pull requests run the quick profile. It should finish in under five minutes. If it doesn’t, raise gctorture’s quick-step or trim quick-containers in the caller workflows; never cut the full profile.
  • A full roadmap stage takes the full-ci label and merges only on a green full run. The roadmap gives the reason in the stage’s **CI.** line, for example first compiled code, a PROTECT or finalizer change, a vendored library, or a Windows-only path.
  • Don’t wait on the full run a merge starts on the default branch, and cancel older full runs it supersedes. A failure that only the full set shows goes on the Full CI stage issue as a comment with the run link, and is fixed there. A failure the quick profile also shows is fixed now.
  • Full CI and v0.1.0 readiness wait for a green full run on their merge commit, and the release commit always needs one.
  • Locally, run gctorture(TRUE) on the code a C change touches when it is cheap; the full run is the authority.

Vendored native code

The design vendors PCRE2, 8-bit with JIT, BSD-3-Clause with the PCRE2 binary-library exception, starting at 10.48 to match vectorscan (design D1). Vendored in Stage 1:

Tag pcre2-10.48
Commit 7978954dbd2efc6f2196869290553cf1871b4ce6
Archive SHA-256 ebcc25aadf2a51fa1fefa9b8bc9e7a79b3dae86870a0f1152a22e42befd46888
Per-file checksums tools/vendor/checksums.sha256
Patches tools/patches/pcre2/, listed in src/vendor/PROVENANCE

src/vendor/PROVENANCE holds the update procedure. tools/vendor/verify checks that the manifest, PROVENANCE, inst/COPYRIGHTS, src/Makevars.in and tests/testthat/test-info.R agree, so a bump that forgets one fails. tests/testthat/test-abi.R is the nm guard: it fails on any exported symbol but R_init_zuregex and on any linked stdio, exit, abort or RNG symbol, on every CI leg.

  • Pin a stable upstream release, never master or a release candidate.
  • Record the tag, the commit and the checksums, and write down the update procedure so the next bump is mechanical.
  • Keep upstream LICENSE and NOTICE under src/vendor/<lib>/, declare the vendored code in DESCRIPTION and inst/COPYRIGHTS.
  • Keep the vendor tree clearly separated from first-party source, and record every local patch and why it exists.
  • CRAN’s compiled-code check applies to vendored code too. No stdout or stderr, no printf, abort, exit or system RNG may be linked, even behind a debug switch that never runs. Remove them with a patch in tools/patches/, list it in src/vendor/PROVENANCE, and make the vendor-verify script check “upstream plus exactly these patches”. Avoid diagnostic-suppressing pragmas too, because they draw their own NOTE. zuhtml is the reference: tools/patches/0002-no-stdio.patch and tools/verify-vendor. zuxml’s first upload was archived because it justified such a symbol instead of patching it.
  • Guard against regressions in CI: run nm -u on the built objects and fail on any of those symbols, so an upstream bump cannot bring them back.

Commits and pull requests

Short, imperative, sentence-case commit subjects, optionally scoped. Keep each commit focused and do not sweep in unrelated files. A pull request explains the user-visible outcome and the rationale, links related issues, lists the checks that were run and the tests that were skipped, and flags platform-sensitive or vendored changes. Performance claims need evidence.

Never commit or push to the default branch. Work on a branch, open a pull request, and leave it for review. Do not merge a pull request unless you are told to.

When you find a defect, in this package or in an upstream tool, open an issue for it rather than only working around it.

Working with skills

The portfolio’s workflow skills live in pedrobtz/r-skills (pkg-init, pkg-roadmap, pkg-implement, pkg-critical-review, pkg-cran-review, pkg-post-cran, pkg-readme); the general process skills are Superpowers. building-a-package.md in pedrobtz/packages walks through them in order. Both sets defer to this file where they overlap, so the settlements are recorded here.

  • One design. The specification is .agents/design.md, adopted from the package’s RFC in pedrobtz/packages/rfcs. A package with an adopted design is past brainstorming; a design change goes through the RFC, not a new spec. Superpowers’ default docs/superpowers/specs/ is not used.
  • Plans at two levels. .agents/roadmap.md holds the stages, one mergeable pull request each, with exit criteria and a CI tier (pkg-roadmap). Inside a stage, writing-plans breaks the work into tasks of one test cycle each, saved as .agents/plans/stage-<n>.md. The roadmap stays authoritative; a plan is scratch and is not kept in sync.
  • Build and merge. pkg-implement runs the stage loop: branch stage-<n>-<slug> from the stage issue, implement the plan with test-driven-development (Rscript -e 'devtools::test(filter = "<name>")' is the red/green command), open the pull request, merge on green at the stage’s CI tier. The confirmation the user gives at the start of that loop is the “told to merge” that Commits and pull requests requires, so the finishing-a-development-branch menu is not presented for stage pull requests. Any other pull request still waits for review.
  • Failures and claims. A failing check or test goes through systematic-debugging before a fix. “Green”, “done” and “ready for CRAN” are claimed only after verification-before-completion: run the command, read the output.
  • Review. requesting-code-review gates tasks inside a stage. pkg-critical-review reviews the whole package once the roadmap is implemented, with Posit’s reviewers, and files issues. CRAN’s reviewer email and GitHub review threads go through receiving-code-review.
  • Keep scratch out of the tarball. R CMD build reads .Rbuildignore, not .gitignore. It must list ^\.agents$, ^\.superpowers$ (the Superpowers task ledger), ^\.worktrees$ (if git worktrees are kept in the package directory; a sibling directory avoids the question), ^\.claude$, ^CLAUDE\.md$, ^AGENTS\.md$, ^CRAN-SUBMISSION$ and ^cran-comments\.md$. A stray top-level file is a NOTE, and the pretest archives on NOTEs.
